why: The reader reaches it by a change of course, not a purpose link. The double track first heads towards King's Pyland (¶122), then turns back and ends at Mapleton's gates (¶124). A man who set out to return a stray and then reversed into the rival stable changed his mind and kept it.

The horse's blow served no aim, so no purpose link can reach it. The reader gets there from what is told: the horse was in the hollow at the struggle (¶37) and left it alone (¶120). Straker was there with an uncorked cataract knife and a struck light (¶82, ¶102), and the sheep were lamed (¶173). A frightened horse's shod hoof is the 'heavy weapon' (¶35).

value: to do something to the horse himself
to do something to him that could not be done in the stall
nobody meant to carry him off: he was led out to be harmed and got loose

why: Who led the horse out is itself open until ¶220, so the reasoning is not a purpose link from a known agent's act. The reader reaches it from what is told: Holmes asks why the horse was not harmed in the stall (¶57). Later come the delicate cataract knife (¶80–81), the cork taken off (¶82), the light struck in the hollow (¶102) and the lamed sheep (¶173). Together they point to a fine cut that needed light and privacy away from the lads in the loft.

The question's agent is unknown until ¶220, so no purpose link from a named agent's act applies. The reader reaches it from what is told: the horse left the hollow alone and nobody led it away (¶120). Brown found it loose afterwards (¶146). The knife, the light and the sheep (¶82, ¶102, ¶173) show it was led out to be lamed, not carried off.

The reader reaches the drugger by elimination over who could choose and reach the dish, not by linking the drugging to its aim. Only Hunter's portion held opium; the household ate the same curry unharmed (¶37). Powdered opium has a taste that a curry hides, and a stranger meeting the maid by chance could not have known the supper would be curry (¶218). So the drugger was one of the two at the house who chose the menu. The dog's silence (¶181–182) and the locked door opened in the night point to Straker as the night visitor, and he needed the lad asleep (¶220).
